dataset: Sourced calculation methodology for an educational pipe-insulation heat loss / heat gain / surface-temperature / condensation calculator modeled on ASTM C680 and NAIMA 3E Plus: outer-surface convection and radiation, air properties, contact-burn (personnel protection) criteria, dew point, condensation-control design margin, saturation vapor pressure, and the heat/mass-transfer analogy.

units.ip: Most C680-style formulas are in inch-pound units exactly as the sources print them: h in Btu/(h*ft^2*F), k in Btu/(h*ft*F) unless marked Btu*in/(h*ft^2*F), lengths in ft (diameters entered in inches and divided by 12), velocity in ft/h (mph*5280), temperatures F, R (=F+459.67) or K as each formula requires.
units.si: Psychrometric and textbook formulas are in SI where the source is SI (Pa, hPa, K, degC, kg/m^2*s).
units.temperature_bases: Each air-property formula below states which temperature scale it takes; mixing them up was the main error class DNV found in a reviewed C680 tool (M3).

conventions.unverified: The literal string 'unverified' means no fetched source stated the value. Nothing was guessed, averaged, converted or filled from memory.
conventions.src: Every fact carries 'src', a list of ids in the top-level 'sources' array.
conventions.quotes: 'quote' strings are verbatim from the source text (pdftotext, HTML-to-text, or source-code lines). Line breaks and table-cell wraps were joined; nothing else changed. HTML sub/superscripts come out as spaced inline text (e.g. 'h r', 'ft 2') and are left that way. Where pdftotext flattened a superscript (e.g. '109' for 10^9) the quote keeps the extracted text and the 'equation' field gives the intended reading. Quotes flagged 'from_image': true were transcribed from a rendered page image because the PDF is scanned or the equation is an image.
conventions.quote_check: The build script checked every quote not flagged 'from_image' against the saved source text (whitespace-insensitive); 'quote_check' records the result.
conventions.c680_paywall: The ASTM C680 text (equations, test cases, C# program) is paywalled. Only the public store pages (M1, M2) were read directly. Unauthorized full-text copies of C680 found by search were deliberately not used. The C680 equations recorded here come from two independent public reproductions: (a) DNV's 2024 C680-23 compliance review tables (M3), which print each formula of a reviewed spreadsheet tool next to DNV's correction notes; DNV states the corrected tool then matched its C680 calculations; and (b) the NIA/NIBS Mechanical Insulation Design Guide calculators' published JavaScript (M8, M10, M12). The two agree. C680 equation numbers are known only where DNV quotes them.
conventions.dnv_table_caveat: M3 Appendix B prints the PRE-correction formulas of the reviewed tool, with DNV notes saying what had to change to match C680 (e.g. use film temperature, use Kelvin, sign of the -12 exponent). The 'c680_reading' fields apply DNV's notes; they agree with the NIA code (M8).
conventions.agent_checks: Values under 'agent_consistency_checks' were computed by the research agent from the sourced formulas. They are cross-checks only, not source values.

method: Sources were downloaded with curl and read with pdftotext (raw and -layout) or an HTML-to-text pass. Scanned PDFs (M16, M18, M20) and equation images (M15 equations, M22 Fig. 2) were rendered with pdftoppm and read visually. Published calculator JavaScript was downloaded and read as text, never executed. PDFs and downloads were kept under /tmp/claude-1000/research-calc/, outside the repo. Tried without success: wbdg.org MIDG pages (now a JavaScript single-page app; curl returns an empty shell; the same MIDG content is hosted by NIA, M5-M11); eng-tips.com C680 thread (HTTP 403); ASHRAE Handbook-Fundamentals ch. 23 and ch. 1 text (subscription only); the CCrall Consulting 2007 report 'Validation of Heat Transfer Calculations in the NAIMA 3EPlus v.4.0 Computer Program' (cited in M3, no public copy found); 3eplus.org web app (calculations run server-side; its JS bundle holds no correlations).

facts.quote: 1.1 This practice provides the algorithms and calculation methodologies for predicting the heat loss or gain and surface temperatures of certain thermal insulation systems that can attain one dimensional, steady- or quasi-steady-state heat transfer conditions in field operations.

1.4 The computer program that can be generated from the algorithms and computational methodologies defined in this practice is described in Section 7 of this practice. The computer program is intended for flat slab, pipe and hollow sphere insulation systems.
However, additional information on effects of wind velocity, jacket emittance, ambient conditions and other influential parameters may also be required to properly select an insulation system.

5.6 The calculation of surface temperature and heat loss or gain of an insulated system is mathematically complex, and because of the iterative nature of the method, computers best handle the calculation.

3E Plus uses the heat flow calculation method described in ASTM C680 titled: Standard Practices for Determination of Heat Gain or Loss and the Surface Temperature of Insulated Piping on Equipment Systems by the Use of a Computer System.
Reliable, repeatable results – Built on ASTM Standard C680 just like previous versions of 3E Plus to deliver clear unbiased results.

In addition to the comments about the pipe insulation tool listed above, DNV verified that 3EPlus results match ASTM- C680 results for horizontal and vertical pipe insulation applications that do not require characteristic length.
The representative at NAIMA provided a validation report that was developed by a company called CCrall Consulting.
This report confirmed that the 3EPlus assumes 10 feet for the characteristic length for all flat vertical surfaces, the geometry type chosen for non-pipe applications.

c680_and_3eplus_relationship.note: ASTM C680-23 (M1) and C680-23a (M2) have identical Scope text. The paywalled full text holds the equations and the C# program; DNV (M3) worked from it and quotes some equation numbers.

facts.quote: The five main input variables are: • Bare surface temperature • Ambient temperature • Wind speed • Surface diameter (or characteristic length for non-pipe geometries) • Pipe surface emissivity

From the input variables, air properties, such as air density, thermal conductivity of air, and kinematic viscosity are calculated. From these air properties, along with the input variables, several dimensionless variables are calculated, such as Prandtl number, Rayleigh number, Reynolds number, and Nusselt number.

The radiation heat transfer coefficient is calculated using the difference between the surface temperature and ambient temperature, and the emissivity of the surface. From the convective and radiative heat transfer coefficients, the total bare heat loss rate is determined.

With the information on the insulation properties, including its thickness, thermal conductivity, and emissivity, and an initial guess at the outer insulation surface temperature (based on the average of the bare surface temperature and the ambient temperature), an iterative process is followed until the guess for the outer surface temperature matches the calculated value for the outer surface temperature.

The previous calculation methodology for insulated pipes and components did not use an iterative process as outlined in the ASTM C680 standard. DNV recommended that the tool be updated to include 3 iterations.

facts.quote: 1.2 The maximum acceptable temperature for a particular surface is derived from an estimate of the possible or probable contact time, the surface system configuration, and the level of injury deemed acceptable for a particular situation.

1.3 For design purposes, the probable contact time for industrial situations has been established at 5 s. For consumer products, a longer (60-s) contact time has been proposed by Wu ( 1 ) 2 and others to reflect the slower reaction times for children, the elderly, or the infirm.
1.4 The maximum level of injury recommended here is that causing first degree burns on the average subject. This type of injury is reversible and causes no permanent tissue damage.
5.3 It is beyond the scope of this guide to establish appropriate contact times and acceptable levels of injury for particular situations, or determine what surface temperature is “safe.”
5.6 This guide is not intended to cover hazards for cold temperature exposure, that is, refrigeration or cryogenic applications.

5.7 The procedure found in this guide has been described in the literature as applicable to all heated surfaces. For extremely high-temperature metallic surfaces (>70°C), damage occurs almost instantaneously upon contact.

facts.quote: 1.1 This practice covers a procedure for evaluating the skin contact temperature for heated surfaces. Two complimentary procedures are presented. The first is a purely mathematical approximation that is used during design or for worst case evaluation. The second method describes the thermesthesiometer, an instrument that analogues the human sensory mechanism and is only used on operating systems.
5.4 Practice C680 is referenced for use with Guide C1055 and Practice C1057 for burn hazard evaluation for heated surfaces.
The potential for burns to human skin is a complex function of surface temperature, surface material, and time of contact.

Standard industry practice is to specify a maximum temperature of 140°F for surfaces that may be contacted by personnel. This temperature would cause no more than first-degree burns for all surfaces for contact times up to about 5 seconds. Note that for non-industrial settings (e.g., retail stores), it may be prudent to design for longer contact times (i.e., using lower surface temperatures).

For outdoor installations, base calculations on summer design ambient temperatures with no wind (i.e., the worst case). Surface temperatures increase because of solar loading but are usually neglected because of variability in orientation, solar intensity, and many other complicating factors.

Note that the choice of jacketing strongly affects a surface's relative safety. Higher-emittance jacketing materials (e.g., plastic, painted metals) can be selected to minimize the surface temperature. Jacketing material also affects the relative safety at a given surface temperature. For example, at 175°F, a stainless-steel jacket blisters skin more severely than a nonmetallic jacket at equal contact time.
In the case of hot insulation, the surface temperature must be limited to below 140F (or more preferably 125F) to protect personnel from potentially irreversible injury.

facts.quote: The design goal is to keep the surface temperature above the dew-point temperature of the surrounding air. Calculating surface temperature is relatively simple, but selecting the appropriate design condition is often confusing. The appropriate design condition is normally the "worst-case" condition expected for the application. For condensation control, however, a design that satisfies the worst-case condition is sometimes impossible.

For outdoor applications (and mechanical rooms vented to outdoor conditions), it is suggested to design for RH of 90%. Appropriate water-resistant, vapor-retarder jacketing or mastics must then be specified to protect the system from the inevitable surface condensation.

Often, the HVAC system will be sized to provide indoor conditions of 75°F/50% RH on a design summer day. However, those indoor conditions would not represent the worst-case indoor conditions with respect to the insulation design.
The insulation system will therefore be designed for an operating temperature of 40°F, an ambient temperature of 81°F, and an ambient RH of 90%.
With a 4 inch NPS, horizontal chilled water pipe, operating at 40°F, in a 90°F ambient with 85% relative humidity and no wind.
